The privatisation of responsibility for water provision changes the social contract
servants have access to clean water at work, even when there is a water shortage at home,

rationale: This qualitative study (ethnographic observations, walking/photographic site visits to 22 apartment buildings and one informal settlement, and interviews with officials, experts, middle-class residents, and domestic workers in Mumbai) examines the municipal policy shift and building-level rainwater-harvesting mandates that transfer responsibility for urban water provision from centralized municipal supply (MCGM) to decentralized private/co-operative residential self-provisioning ('localised privatisation', coded under regulatory_model_ownership, with secondary discussion of plot-size thresholds and tenure insecurity in informal settlements under eligibility_status_documentation). The primary empirical outcomes analyzed across the three case studies are effective_access dimensions: 24-hour supply continuity, resilience to shortages, water quantity for domestic/sanitation tasks, perceived potability/water quality, and gendered water-fetching drudgery.
